messages.author: b4a3b38d0539362f
messages.subject: Maybe off-topic: Tabular: A Schema-Driven Probabilistic Programming Language
parts:
I came across this recent paper from Microsoft Research: Tabular: A Schema-Driven Probabilistic Programming Language and maybe it is of interest to the community. I am an entry level stan user and this whole "probabilistic relational programming language" deal is news to me. 
The wikipedia page on probabilistic relational programming language does not mention stan (but does BUGS). Should stan appear on that page?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maybe off-topic: Tabular: A Schema-Driven Probabilistic Programming Language
parts:
Thanks. I hadn't seen Tabular before (another name that's
going to be hard to search for), nor had I heard of "probabilistic
relational" languages.

The description of what they are on the Wikipedia page:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_relational_programming_language

just pointed to:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_relational_model

Neither Stan nor BUGS seem to fit the model of relational model, which
seems derived from relational databases. But then neither do Dyna or
Factorie, both of which I know form natural language processing. And for
that matter, neither do Church or Infer.NET, both of which are much more
general.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maybe off-topic: Tabular: A Schema-Driven Probabilistic Programming Language
parts:
I think "schema" is synonymous to a certain degree to "model" in addition to "relational schema". In stan's case, the model has attributes organized as columns (rather than the rows of a traditional SQL database), and specifies their type, value constraints, and relationships (either "strong" in the case of transformed data or "weak" in case of modeling statements). 

This seems like "schema" to me? What do you think?

Emil

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maybe off-topic: Tabular: A Schema-Driven Probabilistic Programming Language
parts:
I just read the Tabular paper's examples and descriptions.

I believe by "schema" they just mean a relational schema
of the kind used to define the tables in a database.

Tabular's overall approach reminds me very much of a company called
Prior Knowledge's product, which filled in missing database tables using
some kind of non-parametric Bayesian models. PK was acquired and apparently
dismantled or rebranded by Salesforce --- I can't find anything with
the query ["prior knowledge" site:salesforce.com].

I think I'd need to know Tabular's underlying languages Fun and
Infer.NET in order to actually understand how sampling works.
I don't understand how Church samples, either.

I don't see any evidence in the paper supporting the claim that Tabular
makes it easier for non-statistics-savvy users to build useful models.
By the time the paper gets to IRT models (figure 2), the annotations look
pretty complex. But then we're interested in a different angle ---
building semi-automated tools for statistics-savvy users.

Andrew Gelman kicked off the Stan project by getting us to think about
specifying hierarchical models in a database-like way (he didn't know that's
what he was talking about, but Matt and I did). And we've
talked about it off and on in our meetings ever since --- I think Michael
even has some sketches of how to make it all work in practice.
Linking databases and Stan would be a great project. At least some subset
of these Tabular models could be directly translated to Stan. Especially if
there were some hierarchical examples. It would even be possible to wrap
the I/O to databases in the same way that RStan and PyStan wrap
I/O in the R and Python. Discrete variables would be a challenge, but we
wouldn't have to start there.

- Bob

P.S. As an aside, papers like this stress how isolated machine learning
is from the applied statistics --- the paper cites a machine learning
paper in 2012 as introducing IRT models!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Maybe off-topic: Tabular: A Schema-Driven Probabilistic Programming Language
parts:
On 12/24/13, 1:26 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, Bob, is the stuff you're discussing at all related to this:
> http://probcomp.csail.mit.edu/bayesdb/

Not quite. BayesDB skips the specification/annotation step, so
should be even more amenable to non-statistically-trained users:

BayesDB assumes that each row of your table is a sample from some fixed population or generative process, and
estimates the joint distribution over the columns. BQL then allows you to draw Bayesian inferences about individuals
and about the overall population or process. The estimates are currently provided by CrossCat, a new nonparametric
Bayesian method for analyzing high-dimensional data tables.

They do say you can override the defaults.

As to CrossCat, they say:

CrossCat is a domain-general, Bayesian method for analyzing high-dimensional data tables. CrossCat estimates the full
joint distribution over the variables in the table from the data, via approximate inference in a hierarchical,
nonparametric Bayesian model, and provides efficient samplers for every conditional distribution. CrossCat combines
strengths of nonparametric mixture modeling and Bayesian network structure learning: it can model any joint
distribution given enough data by positing latent variables, but also discovers independencies between the observable
variables.

That really reminds me of what Prior Knowledge were doing.

And it's related to Yajuan's thesis.

I'd rather these authors tried to make what they were doing sound
less brand new and relate it to other things.

Digging into Appendix A, they're using a factor model that's composed
of a mixture of mixtures, both mixing levels controlled by a Dirichlet
process. So it'd be able to non-parametrically fit something like
a generalized multidimensional ideal-point model (I use that example because
you and Jennifer discuss a 2D example in your regression book). They
seem to be overly optimistic about convergence of Gibbs samplers in
practice given the extreme multimodality of these factor models (there's
been some neat work lately in the machine learning literature on
spectral separability conditions for identifying general forms of factor
models, which might be relevant).
> Also see attached paper that describes what they're doing. It reminds me a lot of the "virtual database query" idea
> that I've been yapping about for the past few yearsï¿½ This one could actually be fun to do as a side project, perhaps
> with that NYT programmer guy we've heard about.

Exactly what I was saying, minus the descriptive term "yapping" :-)

- Bob
